procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated 13th January, 2017 of the High Court of Gujarat at Ahmedabad in Civil Revision Application No.76 of 2016.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Respondent No.1 (defendant No.5) filed a Civil Revision Application No. 76/2016 in the High Court of Gujarat at Ahmedabad challenging the Trial Court's order dismissing his application under Order VII Rule 11(d) of CPC for rejection of the plaint. The High Court allowed the application under Order VII Rule 11(d) of CPC filed by respondent No.1 and reversed the decision of the Trial Court, finding that the suit was barred by limitation.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Appellants approached the Supreme Court by way of a special leave petition, challenging the High Court's judgment and order dated 13th January, 2017. The Supreme Court granted special leave and heard the appeal.

issue.issue_text: Whether the issue of a suit being barred by limitation is a triable issue, preventing the rejection of the plaint at the threshold under Order VII Rule 11(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, especially when the plaintiffs plead lack of knowledge of an alleged fraudulent transaction.

facts: The plaintiffs (appellants) filed a suit regarding their ancestral property, alleging that a sale deed from 1996 was fraudulent.
They claimed that their co-owners (defendants) executed the sale deed by forging their thumb impressions and keeping them in the dark about the transaction.
The plaintiffs asserted in their plaint that they had no knowledge of this fraudulent sale deed until 2013 and filed the suit immediately after discovering it.
law: Under Order VII Rule 11(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure, a court can reject a plaint if the suit appears from the statements within the plaint itself to be barred by any law, such as the law of limitation.
To decide an application under this rule, the court must only look at the averments in the plaint, read as a whole.
The defense or pleas raised by the defendant in their written statement are irrelevant at this preliminary stage.
application: The Supreme Court applied the principle that only the plaint's averments are relevant for an Order VII Rule 11(d) application.
The Court noted that the plaintiffs had clearly pleaded that they were unaware of the fraud until 2013 and that their signatures were forged.
Based on these specific averments, the question of when the limitation period actually started to run is not a straightforward matter that can be decided from the face of the plaint.
The plaintiffs' claim of recent knowledge and fraud creates a "triable issue"—a mixed question of fact and law that requires evidence to be presented and examined during a full trial.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that because the plaintiffs' averments about their lack of knowledge of the alleged fraud raised a question of fact, the issue of whether the suit was barred by limitation was a triable issue. Consequently, the plaint could not be rejected at the threshold under Order VII Rule 11(d).

arguments.issue_text: Whether the issue of a suit being barred by limitation is a triable issue, preventing the rejection of the plaint at the threshold under Order VII Rule 11(d) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, especially when the plaintiffs plead lack of knowledge of an alleged fraudulent transaction.
appellant_arguments: The plaint specifically states that the appellants (plaintiffs) only came to know about the fraudulent transaction on 28.09.2013, which constitutes the cause of action.
Whether the suit is actually barred by limitation is a matter of trial that can only be decided after evidence is presented.
When deciding an application under Order VII Rule 11, the court must only consider the averments made in the plaint.
Based solely on the pleadings in the plaint, which assert a recent date of knowledge, it cannot be concluded that the suit is barred by limitation.
respondent_arguments: The suit was filed in 2013, almost 17 years after the registered sale deed was executed in 1996.
This significant delay makes the suit prima facie barred by the law of limitation.
The decision of the High Court (which presumably rejected the plaint) was correct and should be upheld.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When considering an application under Order 7 Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the court must confine its evaluation to the averments in the plaint, and the pleas taken by the defendant in the written statement are wholly irrelevant at that stage.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The issue of whether a suit is barred by the law of limitation is a subject matter for trial and cannot be decided at the threshold under Order VII Rule 11 of the CPC, especially when the determination of this issue depends on evidence. When deciding such an application, the court must confine its examination to the averments made in the plaint only, and the defense raised by the defendant cannot be taken into account. If the pleadings in the plaint, taken at face value, do not show the suit to be barred by limitation, the plaint cannot be rejected.
legal_tests_applied: When deciding an application under Order VII Rule 11, the Court has to just look into the averments made in the plaint only.
The plea or defense raised by the defendant cannot be taken into account at the stage of deciding an application under Order VII Rule 11.
why_respondent_won: Whether the suit is barred by law of limitation or not is a subject matter of trial which can be decided only after taking evidence.
Merely looking at the pleadings in the plaint, it does not come out that the suit is barred by the law of limitation.
The court cannot consider the defendant's submissions regarding the delay of almost 17 years at the stage of an Order VII Rule 11 application, as these are defenses that require a trial.
